title: Notes of Ministry - 49 - December 1976

paragraphs.text: It is believed that the Spirit would give us some impression of the divine objectives. We must determine our objectives according to what God’s objectives are. It is clear that God is giving us remarkable experiences; that is what we prove in every local assembly. The time of the Supper is more precious than ever, the impressions the Lord leaves among His own are richer than ever, and I believe the service Godward is sustained more richly than ever, too.

We see, therefore, how the Lord is preparing us for what is eternal; He is detaching us from everything here. I believe that is His present objective, to secure in us what will go into eternity, and to set us free from what would hinder us from entrance into it. He would free us from every element of worldliness and earthly-mindedness, not only from the evil things, from the unrighteousness things, but from what is earthly, that we may enter into the heavenly. We should be in the constant enjoyment of the heavenly, and entering into the praises of God in the assembly, marked in these days as true worshippers. The Lord Jesus could speak in chapter 4 of this gospel of “true worshippers” who “worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4: 23); that is a great divine objective, “The Father seeks such as his worshippers”.

But I read this passage because it shows how the Lord is preparing His disciples for this wonderful time of the Spirit. God would give us to value this most wonderful time in His ways with men here. It is a time when Christ is gone to the Father, and when the Spirit is come from Him to be here with the saints and in the saints. The Lord is preparing His disciples for that time. You can see how all His thoughts are focused upon the time that came into view when He came out of death, when He said, “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”, John 20: 17. What a remarkable time that introduced; it is with us still, and the Lord would use these remarks in this passage to give us an impression of what this time of the Spirit is. I believe that would be His objective in this meeting. We need to see that the Lord would have an objective in every meeting; He is not moving among His own without purpose and definiteness. He is moving amongst us with definite ends in mind.

So He says, “I have yet many things to say to you, but ye cannot bear them now”. The Spirit was not yet come. The disciples were there. Jesus was there. Himself the expression of the precious truth, but the Spirit was not yet come, so He says, “Ye cannot bear them now”. But then He says, “But when he is come, the Spirit of truth, he shall guide you into all the truth”. That marks this present time. The Spirit of truth is come in answer to the Lord’s word, and He is guiding the saints into all the truth. We have noticed that expression, “all the truth”. It would remind us that there is no aspect of the truth about which the Spirit is not able to speak to us. Are we ready to be guided? Are we marked by holy energy to come into the truth, the wonderful truth which the Lord has brought in through the Spirit? Do we value this remarkable revival during the past one hundred and fifty years?—a

remarkable action of the Spirit. We are made to realise that in that revival the whole truth has been in view. We see how men who laboured for God among the saints have embraced in scope the whole truth, reflecting the service of the blessed Spirit. God has an objective, and the objective is to secure His saints in full sympathy with all His thoughts.

How wealthy the truth of God is! Remarkable features of the truth have been opened up to us. I think, for example, of the truth of eternal life, which was contended for in 1890 and later years. What have we made of the truth of eternal life? Do we know the experience of eternal life? I quote that as an example of the great wealth of truth that has been opened up to the saints. Have we understood the truth as to the Person of Christ as Son? Have we answered to the truth of liberty to address the blessed Spirit? Have we learned to give Him His full place? These are remarkable elements of the truth, but the Spirit has guided the saints into them. It is a guiding; it supposes a readiness to move on the part of each of us. Are we willing today to move into the full extent of the truth? It will require sacrifice on our part, but how richly rewarded that sacrifice is as the whole heavenly truth is opened out, and as we see where the assembly belongs, where Christ is.

We prove the great supply in divine love, the supply of that by which the saints are sustained; but do we know the love itself? There is love in the Father’s heart, a love that is in the heart of Christ, the love of the Christ for the assembly, love that is evident in the Spirit’s service, love that is brought about in the hearts of the saints. What a realm of love we are brought into! That love would have in mind holiness too. Love and

holiness go very closely together. It is in holy conditions that love is enjoyed; that love becomes the great stimulus to maintain what is holy and according to God. What do we know of these things? Thank God, I believe we do know them, but we see that the Lord’s objective is to bring us into them in a yet fuller way.

It says of the Spirit, “he shall not speak from himself; but whatsoever he shall hear he shall speak”. Then the Lord speaks of the Father’s things; He says that they are His things too. What wonderful things the Lord is speaking about, bringing into view what we speak of as the economy of love—the Son in relation with the Father, but the Spirit in relation with the Father and the Son, a glorious economy in which we can know the Father and the Son and the Spirit. Then we can respond, speaking to the Father, speaking to the Son, speaking to the Spirit, speaking to God in the assembly in all His blessedness and greatness. What wonderful subjects we have, beloved brethren, affording such scope for worshipping hearts, and the divine objective is to bring us into these things. The Lord is speaking to His beloved disciples in the intimacy and privacy with which He was with them; the adverse power of the Jews was very close, and soon He would be betrayed and put to death, but the Lord is showing what His objective is, to bring His saints into the choicest and best.

It is said at that time that He had many things to say to them, but they could not bear them yet; but we, dear brethren, are in this time in which all the divine thoughts for men are being disclosed. Through the Spirit’s grace we can bear them. The Lord said, “Ye cannot bear them now”, but the time is come in which they can be borne. The Lord would go away, as He says, “A little while and ye do not behold me; and again a little while and ye shall

see me”. That is the time in which we are. The Lord says, “Ye shall see me, because I go away to the Father”. The Lord had His going to the Father in view. Now He has gone to the Father. What a message of triumph it was which He sent by Mary, “I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”. The time for that came when the Lord had triumphed over death, bringing in resurrection and ascension, among the greatest thoughts of God. We could not bear these things without the Spirit, but the Spirit is come now that we may enter into them. The divine thought is that we should enter into them; that is, might I say, His objective in this very meeting. This is very much on the side of privilege.

What we have in Revelation relates to our responsibility. The Lord is speaking to the assemblies, appealing to responsible persons in them. He is speaking plainly about the real conditions that He finds. He is showing that He can deal with those conditions. Then in each of the seven assemblies He refers to the overcomer—a most encouraging feature, because it shows that He has prominently in mind that negative conditions shall be overcome. If there are negative conditions the overcomer will overcome them. It is very remarkable how the Lord speaks to the overcomers, but it is part of the Lord’s objective that we stand as overcomers in every kind of adverse circumstance. There are many negative conditions referred to in these seven epistles, but in respect of all the overcomer is presented to us. What an Overcomer Jesus was!—“I have overcome”, as He says in another passage (John 16: 33), and how hearts true to Christ would strive to overcome. The Lord makes plain what is to be overcome. We have all noticed how very plainly the Lord speaks in these seven letters; with love and with skill

He deals with the negative things, and with appreciation He speaks of the positive things; but He shows what the real conditions are—for the Lord is doing that, He is showing us what the real conditions are so that He may bring the overcomer into view. I believe this is a very current matter in many parts of the world where conditions exist which for the time being are difficult.

There is a wealth of appeal in the Lord’s word, “Hold fast what thou hast”; how much, beloved brethren, God has given us. What a wonderful revival He has called us into! But He is seeking to preserve us fully in it; He would also strengthen our sense of responsibility— that is a very important point. The Lord would strengthen our sense of responsibility that we may stand faithful to Him and to every thought of God. So the Lord says, “Hold fast what thou hast”; let no diversion come in. Let us hold it fast. One thing the enemy is attacking is the truth as to separation. We find the enemy would have us have some part in all kinds of things that dishonour Christ, but the Lord would have us to be overcomers. He would make this very attractive to us in this meeting that we may appear as overcomers who answer to His word “Hold fast what thou hast”. These matters of separation, dear brethren, are not new ones. Some speak of them as if they were introduced not many years ago. These are not new things. We go back in the history of the recovery and see how current they were many, many years ago. I say that by way of practical warning, that we may remain true to Christ, true to the One who loved us and gave Himself for us. The Lord would reach deeply into our affections at such a time and say, “Hold fast what thou hast, that no one take thy crown”. The crown, I suppose, is the crown of reward for faithful continuance to the end in the light of every divine thought as to the

assembly. Let us allow no divine thought to fail. Let us not be found lacking in faithfulness to Christ and faithfulness to the truth. The enemy draws very near sometimes; he would seek to take this crown away; but let every heart true to Christ resolve that it shall be held fast, as Christ’s lovers continue in faithfulness to the end.

I do not speak of them in detail, but there are wonderful promises to the overcomer. Read them, and see what wonderful objectives the Lord has, and relate it especially to the divine glory and the divine thoughts in their full extent. One great thought which comes into view at the end is the city, ready for eternity. We can see this as the great objective in the divine mind, for God in His faithful love shows us the objective. He would give us those verses (Revelation 21: 2, 3) to engage us with what is going into eternity in the assembly. What a vessel the assembly is in His sight! This is to attract our hearts to the wealth of God’s objective, and to keep this objective before us at the present time, that it may constantly affect us, constantly elevate our thoughts, and strengthen us in a heavenly course that is proper to God’s assembly. Can we link anything unclean with such a vessel as this? Can we link anything earthly with such a vessel as this? We are given briefly, but powerfully, a view of the assembly where God reaches His ultimate thought—“The tabernacle of God is with men”. This is His ultimate objective, beloved brethren, and we see how it is reached and carried through in the assembly, all on the basis of what God’s glorious Son has effected, and that through the service of the blessed Spirit; but it all brings through in a heavenly vessel a full answer to divine thoughts. This is the ultimate objective, a vessel in which God Himself is glorified and in which everything of Him is carried into eternity.

So may we have the divine objectives before us, the Lord’s thoughts as to this wonderful time of the Spirit, the appeal to us as to our responsibilities, “Hold fast what thou hast, that no one take thy crown”, and then the ultimate objective of God in view of His eternal glory. May we be found answering to these things, for His name’s sake.
P. van den Berg
Proverbs 4: 1–6; Mark 15: 21; 16: 3–5; 2 Timothy 2: 1–8

I would like to speak about the continuation of the testimony, and I have particularly in mind the way the older and the younger go together. There are not any separate classes in the assembly. Whether we are young or old, if we have accepted the Lord Jesus as our own personal Saviour and have the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit, we are all set together in one body, and we are all brethren. In that way we are all together in the same relationship and that is one of the greatest things we can think of, spiritual relationships, in which we have through grace been put together. When we think of the testimony we think of the generation that is passing, and another generation that is coming. Many have laboured and have gone to be with the Lord, and we are thankful

for the faithfulness of many that have gone before us, who have served the Lord in their generation and have gone to be with Him. We can thank God for fathers and mothers who have been given to us; but they will go, and the burden of the testimony will fall on us. It is of all importance that older ones and younger ones should move together. It is wonderful to be in the flock, to be the subjects of the Lord’s own care, to enjoy the Lord’s provision, to have fatherly and motherly instruction.

The writer of The Proverbs was a son unto his father, tender and an only one in the sight of his mother, and he addresses particularly the younger generation on the line of experience. We have been speaking about making a collection (see Ecclesiastes 12: 11), and it is very important that we should lay up treasures in heaven, and that we have a treasure in our own hearts. The greatest treasure, of course, is the Lord Jesus Himself. God has given great treasure in that blessed Person. Paul says, “How shall he not also with him grant us all things?”, Romans 8: 32. The Father has opened His heart and has opened His house, He has opened His treasures; there is a great inheritance opened to us and it is for us all, old and young, to lay hold of it. Paul is particularly concerned about the continuation of the testimony in the way he writes to Timothy. He writes to him as to laying hold of “what is really life”, 1 Timothy 6: 19. There are a lot of things that are not really life. You will find that spiritual prosperity comes when you lay hold of what is really life. There are many things that are not wrong in themselves which are not really life, and if we are unduly occupied with them we shall miss the very best that God wants to give us to enjoy.
So one is concerned about spiritual prosperity

amongst us. The pleasure of Jehovah prospers in the hand of the Lord Jesus, and we have, in type, the Son of the Father’s love speaking in Proverbs. In chapter 6: 20 he says, “My son, observe thy father’s commandment, and forsake not the teaching of thy mother; bind them continually upon thy heart”. Just bind on your heart what we have received in these days together, and then “tie them about thy neck—when thou walkest, it shall lead thee …”. That means that you receive spiritual adornment in the teaching that comes to us. It is very beautiful to have such adornment, a meek and quiet spirit, which is precious to God. “When thou sleepest, it shall keep thee; and when thou awakest, it shall talk with thee. For the commandment is a lamp, and the teaching a light, and reproofs of instruction are the way of life”. All this is connected with the kingdom of the Son of the Father’s love. As you are enjoying the wonderful light that is shining it will preserve you from both the darkness, and the authority of darkness, which surround you.

Now it is very wonderful to see how Abraham and Isaac move together. There is the older generation and there is the younger generation. Isaac says, “My father”, and Abraham says, “My son”, and they two went on together (Genesis 22: 7, 8). We see the same in Elijah and Elisha. Elijah was going away and Elisha was the fresh generation, to continue the testimony, and they two go on together. It is not that Elisha is not tested; there were four moves which were a test to Elisha, but he was not prepared to part with Elijah, and the two went on together (2 Kings 2: 4–3). Oh how our hearts yearn that we may all go on together! In Matthew’s gospel the testimony is going on to the end. It is very interesting to see in that gospel how the Lord takes up the ass and the colt and how He sat

on them (Matthew 21: 7). The Lord takes on the two generations, and that is how the testimony is carried through. One generation is going, another is coming, and together they carry the burden of the testimony. They carry the Lord in testimony.

When we come to Mark’s gospel the colt only is mentioned. Mark was a young man and he had gone with Paul to the work of the Lord, then he missed his way and went back to Jerusalem. But it is wonderful what Mark experienced in the way of grace and the way he was recovered. Paul at the end could say, “Take Mark, and bring him with thyself, for he is serviceable to me for ministry”, 2 Timothy 4: 11. Here was a young man who was available for the continuation of the testimony; like all of us, he had been recovered. So Mark would understand, in speaking about the colt, the Lord’s concern about the younger generation for they were to carry on the testimony and needed to be set free. They are bound and, in a sense, we can thank God for certain limitations that are upon us, but the time comes when the Lord claims us; it is then we are needed. The time has come, I believe, when the Lord is in need of the younger ones. We are very thankful to hear young brothers in the meetings—and that does not, of course, mean that the young sisters are not needed in the testimony. All are needed, sisters and brothers.

The whole epistle to the Romans was written in order to commend one sister, Phoebe, “minister of the assembly which is in Cenchrea” (Romans 16: 1), and Paul speaks of those women “who have contended along with me in the glad tidings”, Philippians 4: 3. Then we find women ministering to the Lord of their substance. How important is the part of the sisters in the bearing of the burdens of the testimony! So that in Luke a young man and a young woman are raised up.

It says of the young man whom Jesus raised that he “began to speak” (Luke 7: 15), and when the Lord raised up the damsel He commanded they should give her something to eat (Luke 8: 55). So it is not just for the young brothers, but for the young sisters also. Both must receive spiritual food in order to have spiritual substance to communicate to others. Now we can understand how Mark writes with a sense of grace in being recovered. He would feel that he lost his garment at a critical juncture in the testimony, because he was not properly girded with the truth. The young man in Mark 14: 52 had a linen garment but he did not appear to have a girdle. We must not hold the truth loosely, but we must needs be strengthened and have our loins girded with the truth, that we may keep our garment, and be available for priestly service.

Both Mark and Luke were available to Paul at the end of his testimony, and were available to continue in the light of Paul’s ministry. That is what I desire to stress. Both on the prophetic line, as in Mark, and the priestly conflict, as in Luke’s gospel, there is need for the young ones, and for us all, to be identified unreservedly with the sufferings of the testimonial position here. I am sure that if the older generation is identified with the cross of Jesus, if Simon the Cyrenian is here, there is bound to be a generation available in the testimony, because this Simon is said to be the father of Alexander and Rufus. No doubt they were known among the brethren, and they had a father who carried the cross of Jesus. You young people have parents who have identified themselves with the testimony, and the Lord wants you to be identified with the testimonial setting here. We may feel weak, but the Lord has provided for that. He knows our hearts and our desires; He knows we

want to follow Him, and following the Lord Jesus means bearing His cross. He is a wonderful Friend to help us and be with us. He will never, never let us down. His wonderful grace is available for all our weakness. If I am to follow in this way I feel nothing but weakness, and then the Lord Jesus comes and says, “My grace suffices thee; for my power is perfected in weakness”, 2 Corinthians 12: 9.

So we find there is a young man in the sepulchre in Mark. However much we may have failed, the answer to it is what God has secured in resurrection, in which we have justification. When we come to resurrection there is no failure; everything liable to fail is finished in the death of Christ. Everything needed for God in the continuation of the testimony is secured in resurrection. So the women say, ‘Who shall roll away the stone?’. How will the testimony go through? Will the testimony go through? Yes, it will go through; the stone is rolled away. If the testimony is to go through God has angels to make way for it. Have you ever thought of the service of angels? They are servants of those who are heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1: 14). They are particularly interested in the children. You can count on angelic help. You may say, ‘What will the school teacher say?’. You see things that are in the way, and you do not see your path clearly. God will clear the way for you. God can clear the way for the youngest amongst us. These women could not roll away the stone; you could not roll away that stone; an angel rolled away the stone (Matthew 28: 2). There is a young man in the grave clothed in a white robe. Is that not wonderful? I think that Mark really experienced it and that thus he was serviceable to Paul for ministry.
So Paul in writing to Timothy says, “Remember Jesus Christ raised from among the dead”. Here is

a young brother. Timothy, and Paul says to him, “Thou therefore, my child, be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus”. Not, ‘Be strong in yourself’; you cannot rely on your own strength. The Lord says, “Without me ye can do nothing”, John 15: 5. Peter was weak when he trusted in his own strength. But when, in your weakness, you trust in the Lord Jesus, you find He is a wonderful Priest who gives you grace. Paul says, “Be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus. And the things thou hast heard of me in the presence of many witnesses, these entrust to faithful men, such as shall be competent to instruct others also”. That is the continuation of the testimony. Here is another generation in Timothy. Timothy and Paul went on together. Paul’s ways were in Christ and Timothy reminded the Corinthians of Paul’s ways. They two went on together, and Paul says, “Take thy share in suffering as a good soldier of Jesus Christ”. Timothy had a father in Paul who, in principle, bore the cross of Jesus, and Paul had a spiritual generation in which the testimony was continued. That is the concern of the moment, that we may be fully available in the continuation of the testimony.

We do not know when the Lord Jesus will come, but Paul is writing here feeling he was about to go. He had combated the good combat, he had kept the faith, and now Timothy was to carry on as a good soldier himself, and other faithful men are called on. Paul speaks of not being entangled with the affairs of life. Have your ‘collection’ where neither moth nor rust destroys. Have a good treasure in your own heart so that you may be able to stand in an evil day, and be available for the completion of the testimony. Take your full share in it. Ask the Lord to give you increased desire; He loves to give you the desires of your heart. Paul, as a father, exhorts Timothy to be occupied with these things so that his progress may be

manifest to all (1 Timothy 4: 15). So you gather up in your treasury fresh things all the time, and in the part that you take in the service of God there will be increase and freshness. How wonderful to see how Samuel developed in the temple, how he grew, and what motherly concern there was for him. Every year his mother brought him a little coat and every time she came it would be a larger one; there was spiritual increase (1 Samuel 2: 21).

May the Lord encourage our younger ones—may He encourage us all—in view of the continuation of the testimony, to be fully committed to it. Paul says to Timothy, “Be not therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner”, 2 Timothy 1: 8. The present testimony, which is the Lord’s, carries this distinct feature that it is bound up with the ministry of the apostle Paul. May we all be fully committed to it, for His name’s sake.

There is always a need for reliable young men and women. In the scripture read it seems that the difficulty between these two great men. Paul and Barnabas, was Mark. He was a younger man who had gone back previously from the work. One does not want to call attention to difficulties and going back, except to encourage the hearts of all that we

should go forward and not go back. As to the work, the apostle tells us elsewhere that we are to be always abounding in the work of the Lord (1 Corinthians 15: 58); the Lord would have us to have our part in relation to His work and not go back from it. There have been many in the past few years who have gone back from the work, but nevertheless it is a day of recovery and we see that at the end Mark was recovered; so we would look for recovery. Many young men have been lost, good young men we might say, but we look for recovery. The great thing at the present time would be that we should not go back from the work; young and old are to be moving together, always abounding in the work of the Lord, and fully committed in relation to what He is doing through His servants.

We see, on the one hand, that Barnabas took Mark and sailed away to Cyprus. That is all it says as to him. Who could question him? He is a servant of the Lord; to his own Master he stands or falls. But we find that Paul, having chosen Silas, had a companion in the work, and he went forth “committed by the brethren to the grace of God”. So Paul had the full fellowship of the saints in all that he did. On that line there would be the support of the Lord in a definite way, and we find that the Lord was supporting Paul in a particular sense at this time. He passed through Syria and Cilicia confirming the assemblies. We see, too, the feature of reliability in Silas whom Paul had chosen. We read of Silas earlier in the chapter. What a man he was! He had the full confidence of the brethren in Jerusalem and he himself was a prophet able to exhort the brethren with much discourse (Acts 15: 32). He was suitable to be a reliable companion of Paul.
We can see it was not an easy thing to be a

companion of Paul in those days as we think of all he had to pass through by way of suffering and opposition. In one sense we can understand how Mark was turned aside; not that that was any excuse for him. But with Silas we find one who was fully committed, so that in chapter 16 we find him side by side suffering with Paul. We can think of him sitting in the inner prison, with his feet fast in the stocks. We think of Paul being there, and we think of Silas being there, side by side with Paul. So I think we need to be side by side, as it were, with Paul and with the testimony, as the Lord may be supporting it at the present time. We are to be whole-hearted in our committal in that sense.

I read on to the next chapter because there we have another young man. Mark was a young man who was turned aside but, in the case of Timotheus, we see that Paul finds him. It says that “he came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there, by name Timotheus”. It does not say here that he was a young man, but undoubtedly he was young because in 1 Timothy 4: 12 the apostle says, “Let no one despise thy youth”. Timothy was to behave himself in such a way that, although he was young, his youth would not be despised. So Timothy is called attention to here, and his surroundings, and it says, “Him would Paul have go forth with him”. I think we would greatly desire that young and old may move together at the present time. We are thankful for older brethren, those with experience. There are many experienced men, experienced servants, amongst us. How we should value them, and we would desire that the younger men may move along with the older ones, that there should be nothing on their side that would call in question their reliability.
I think we could say that Timothy was a reliable young brother, whom Paul could take on, and so he

would have him go forth with him. He took him, and it says that they passed through the cities, instructing the brethren to observe the decrees determined on by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. These two reliable men were moving together with the apostle and it adds that the assemblies “were confirmed in the faith, and increased in number every day”. There is a great desire that the saints in the assemblies might be confirmed in the faith at the present time and increased in number. This, I think, is a feature which we can happily say is taking place. Without saying too much in regard of it, this character of things (whilst recognising the breakdown) is something which is, through divine grace, proceeding at the present time. We greatly desire that it might increase, that the assemblies might be confirmed in the faith and held together as the result of reliable ministry, and reliable men, being found amongst us.

I read that one verse in 2 Timothy because it brings in Mark, “Take Mark, and bring him with thyself, for he is serviceable to me for ministry”. This is a word to Timothy. In one sense Timothy, I suppose, had replaced Mark, but now Mark is recovered. So it is a day of recovery, and we are greatly desirous that there might be much in the way of recovery, young men coming in, and not only young men but others are to be brought in. It says, “Take Mark, and bring him with thyself, for he is serviceable to me for ministry”. So there is much that can be brought in through recovered men. Think of what was brought in through Mark; what a gospel he was able to write! The one who had himself failed as a servant was able to write a gospel in relation to the Servant who never failed. What an appreciation Mark had of Christ! So as we have persons being recovered, they are able to bring in much for the enrichment of the assembly. The two,

we might say, go along together, Timothy and Mark; how happily and definitely they would move together in relation to divine interests! The continuance of the testimony depends in one sense on the younger men and women. So it is important that they should be strengthened in relation to the truth and become reliable, thus helping forward all that is proceeding in relation to the work of the Lord at the present time.

It is interesting that Paul’s ministry goes on to the rapture. We are often comforted by the fact that his ministry particularly bears on our day. We have the second epistle to Timothy and Paul’s ministry bearing on the Lord’s coming, and on the saints as being here just before His coming. So we have this expression twice in the verses read, “We, the living, who remain to the coming of the Lord”, indicating that Paul’s ministry applies right on to the end—a glorious end. We could think of these words as involving not only what is literal, but also what is spiritual. We might say, rightly, that it involves that these persons have not died; but the words themselves are of interest, because Paul’s words are inspired by the Spirit of God, and they are of moment. The apostle uses these words as to those who are living, persons who remain to the coming of the Lord, and they are repeated for

our comfort. The word of God always has its edge, too, so that clearly it is in mind that there is a collective “we”, and they are living and remaining to the coming of the Lord, preserved in the gain and joy of the truth until He comes.

Then the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with an assembling shout. It links with what we had on Lord’s day as to the Lord assembling with His own (Acts 1: 4). This scripture says, “If we believe that Jesus has died and has risen again ...”. After His rising He assembled with His own, but He will come again to the living who remain to His coming. Those who have fallen asleep through Jesus will also be caught up, but I am impressed, beloved brethren, as to what will be here just before the rapture. The Lord will then have what is here for Himself; He will have the “we”, those who are living and remaining.

The moral features that mark them come out in chapter 5. They do not sleep as the rest do; “So then do not let us sleep as the rest do, but let us watch and be sober”. These are moral features that would mark those who are living and remaining to the coming of the Lord. Watchfulness is peculiarly a feature for the last days, watching for our Lover to return with an assembling shout. Also, Paul says, “putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and as helmet the hope of salvation”. These spiritual qualities of faith, love, and hope marked the assemblies in Ephesus and Colosse. Faith, love, and hope will no doubt be found when the Lord comes, and we are to be exercised to put them on. Then it says, “Because God has ... set us ... for obtaining salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who has died for us, that whether we may be watching or sleep, we may live together with him”. Again the word ‘watching’ comes in. I think these three features that enter into these scriptures should mark us at the present time because of the imminence of the Lord’s coming—that we are living, and remaining, and watchful.

Then the apostle in the second epistle touches on “our gathering together to him”; that is the final thing. We had on Lord’s day, “Amen; come, Lord Jesus”, Revelation 22: 20. That will be the answer. He says, “Yea, I come quickly”. He makes the move. The time is in the Father’s hands; times and seasons are in the Father’s authority; but then the Lord comes with His own assembling shout, and then there is this final answer, and our gathering together to Him. May we be ready for it, beloved brethren, for His name’s sake.

Let me ask you, are you sensible of the gravity of division? The assembly cannot be divided as a field. In a division the Head cannot go with both parts. The Lord goes with one side only—He cannot go with both. Then the issue is very solemn, and be assured, if the Lord be not with you, though you may preserve a fair character and an unblemished reputation, and though you may be blessed in the gospel, your light and knowledge of His mind is sure to wane. I have seen it over and over that even godly souls when they lose the presence of the Lord in their midst never receive any fresh light from Him. They are alive but dwarfs. The Lord give you to seek His way at this time.
paragraphs.source: J. B. Stoney (‘Letters to Labourers’, p.280, 1899 Edit.).

paragraphs.text: Upon the holy mount apart
Was seen, revealed to human gaze,
The Object of the Father’s heart,
The Son, unique, beyond all praise.
O glorious Man in whom now rest
God’s purposes and counsels blest,
Himself the Yea and the Amen
To all God’s promises for men.
And, greater still, unveiled we see
God’s thoughts from all eternity
To head up all in Him, the Son,
Marked out as His beloved One.
No single purpose of God’s will
But Christ shall gloriously fulfil
Full actuality to come,
But all assured in that blest One.
The richest thoughts of love divine
Now in resplendent glory shine—
Christ’s brethren, and His heavenly bride,
Israel restored and glorified.
The nations blest and in their place,
A universe secured through grace;
Annulled for ever death’s dark thrall,
New heaven and earth, God all in all.
Now silence falls upon the scene;
One voice is heard, sublime, serene,
Hark!—“This is my beloved Son”—
The Father rests in that blest One.

John in his gospel presents the Lord Jesus immediately as an object of worship—“the Word was with God, and the Word was God”, John 1: 1. Throughout his gospel the verity of the Lord’s manhood and of His deity are wondrously put together, for example, in the Lord’s own reference in chapter 3 to “the Son of man who is in heaven” (John 3: 13), and then in chapter 6—“If then ye see the Son of man ascending up where he was before” (John 6: 62). He who speaks of Himself as Son of man is both truly Man and truly God. Paul speaks thus of the Christ, “who is over all, God blessed for ever”, Romans 9: 5. He has taken His place at the right hand of the greatness on high. The blind man in John 9, then seeing, worships Him when here in blood and flesh. Thomas worships Him in resurrection, exclaiming, “My Lord and my God”, John 20: 28. It is our privilege to worship Him now upon the throne, as it says, “for he is thy Lord, and worship thou him”, Psalm 45: 11.
Kingston, Ont.
